exam_points: Pregnancy: 40 weeks from LMP, 38 weeks from fertilisation.

Weeks 21-25: surfactant begins; weeks 26-29: viability.

Term 37-40 wk; preterm < 37; post-term > 42.
LBW < 2500 g; SGA < 10th percentile; IUGR = failure to reach growth potential.

deeper.title: Why surfactant timing decides survival
deeper.html:
Alveoli are tiny, wet bubbles; without surfactant their surface tension makes them collapse at every breath out. Type II pneumocytes start secreting surfactant around weeks 21-25, but enough is present only later, which is why very preterm babies develop respiratory distress syndrome. Giving the mother corticosteroids when preterm birth is expected speeds up surfactant production, and synthetic surfactant can be given into the baby's trachea after birth. These two measures moved the practical limit of viability earlier.

Source: the lecture's weeks 21-29; standard neonatal practice.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Mesoderm: skeleton, muscle, dermis, urogenital system, serous membranes, heart, blood, spleen, adrenal cortex.
Somites: first segmentation; their number dates the embryo; ~42-44 pairs by week 5.
Somites → axial skeleton, its muscles and dermis.
Folding (week 4): median plane (head, tail) and horizontal plane (lateral).
Head fold: heart and pericardial coelom ventral; septum transversum caudal to heart; foregut.
Tail fold: connecting stalk and allantois ventral; hindgut.
Lateral folds: body walls; midgut linked to yolk sac by vitelline duct.
Intraembryonic coelom → pericardial, pleural, peritoneal cavities.
Haematopoiesis: yolk sac 3-8 wk, liver 6 wk-birth, spleen 10-28 wk, marrow from 18 wk.
Weeks 4-8 = organogenesis, most sensitive to teratogens (e.g. alcohol).

deeper.title: Why the heart ends up in the chest
deeper.html:
Before folding, the heart-forming (cardiogenic) mesoderm lies cranial to the oropharyngeal membrane and the neural plate, at the very front of the disc. As the brain grows rapidly and the head fold swings the cranial end under, the heart and pericardial cavity rotate 180° to lie ventral to the foregut, with the septum transversum now below them. That septum later forms part of the diaphragm, which is why the phrenic nerve comes from the neck (C3-C5): the diaphragm's tissue began life at cervical levels and descended with folding.

Source: the lecture's fate of the head fold; the link to the phrenic nerve from Anatomy.

exam_points: Somatic cells: mitosis, diploid (46); gametes: meiosis, haploid (23).
Meiosis I separates homologues (crossing-over); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Spermatogenesis starts at puberty in seminiferous tubules; sperm mature in the epididymis.
Spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte (2n, 4N) → secondary (n) → spermatid → spermatozoon.

Follicles: primordial → primary → secondary → Graafian (antrum).

One ovum + polar bodies per oocyte; four sperm per spermatocyte.
Capacitation (5-7 h) enables the acrosome reaction; fertilisation in the ampulla.

deeper.title: Why maternal age raises the risk of trisomy
deeper.html:
Primary oocytes enter meiosis I before birth and wait in prophase I until the month they ovulate, up to 40-50 years later. During that long pause the cohesion that holds homologues together weakens, so at ovulation a pair is more likely to fail to separate (non-disjunction). A secondary oocyte carrying an extra chromosome 21, fertilised by a normal sperm, gives trisomy 21. Sperm, made continuously from puberty, do not have this long arrest, which is why the risk rises mainly with the mother's age.

Source: the lecture's timeline of oogenesis; standard link to non-disjunction.

deeper.title: Folic acid and the 28-day window
deeper.html:
The neural tube closes by about day 28 after fertilisation, often before a woman knows she is pregnant. Folate is needed for the rapid DNA synthesis of the folding neuroepithelium, and adequate folate before and early in pregnancy greatly lowers the risk of anencephaly and spina bifida. Because closure is complete so early, supplements must start before conception; starting at the first antenatal visit is often too late. Open defects also leak alpha-fetoprotein, which is why a raised AFP in maternal serum or amniotic fluid prompts a detailed scan.

Source: the lecture's neuropore timing; public-health folate guidance.

deeper.title: Malrotation and the green vomit emergency
deeper.html:
If the midgut does not complete its 270° rotation, the caecum stays high and the small bowel mesentery keeps a narrow base, anchored only near the superior mesenteric artery. That short pivot lets the whole midgut twist around the artery: midgut volvulus. The duodenum is kinked, so a baby vomits bile (green), and the twisted vessels can kill the entire midgut within hours. That is why bilious vomiting in a newborn is treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise, and why the embryology of rotation matters on the ward.

Source: the lecture's midgut rotation and non-rotation anomalies.

deeper.title: Why the zona pellucida must disappear on time
deeper.html:
The zona pellucida keeps the cleaving embryo from sticking to the tubal wall. It has to dissolve ('hatching') once the blastocyst reaches the uterine cavity so the trophoblast can touch the endometrium. If transport is delayed, for example by tubal scarring after infection, the blastocyst hatches while still in the tube and implants there: an ectopic pregnancy. The tube cannot stretch or form a decidua, so it may rupture and bleed, which is why a missed period, pain and a low, slowly rising β-hCG need urgent assessment.

Source: the lecture's role of the zona pellucida and ectopic pregnancy.

deeper.title: Why the fetus needs to breathe liquid
deeper.html:
From about week 10 the fetus makes breathing movements that move amniotic fluid in and out of the airways. The fluid, and the lung's own secretions kept in by the larynx, keep the developing airways distended, and that stretch is a key signal for lung growth and branching. With too little fluid (oligohydramnios from renal agenesis or a long leak), the chest is also compressed by the uterus and the lungs stay small: pulmonary hypoplasia, the usual cause of death in Potter sequence. It is a neat link between the kidneys and the lungs.

Source: the lecture's functions of amniotic fluid and oligohydramnios complications.

deeper.title: Reading chorionicity on an early scan
deeper.html:
Whether twins share a chorion matters more than whether they are identical, because a shared placenta can connect their circulations and cause twin-to-twin transfusion. It is easiest to judge before about 14 weeks: a thick dividing membrane with a triangular 'lambda' wedge of placenta between the sacs means two chorions, while a thin membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle ('T sign') means one. Monochorionic twins are then scanned every two weeks to catch transfusion early.

Source: the lecture's twin membranes; standard obstetric practice.
